abstract.text: Mammalian cells use a complex network of redox-dependent processes necessary to maintain cellular integrity during oxidative metabolism, as well as to protect against and/or adapt to stress. The disruption of these redox-dependent processes, including those in the mitochondria, creates a cellular environment permissive for progression to a malignant phenotype and the development of resistance to commonly used anticancer agents. An extension of this paradigm is that when these mitochondrial functions are altered by the events leading to transformation and ensuing downstream metabolic processes, they can be used as molecular biomarkers or targets in the development of new therapeutic interventions to selectively kill and/or sensitize cancer versus normal cells. In this Review we propose that mitochondrial oxidative metabolism is altered in tumor cells, and the central theme of this dysregulation is electron transport chain activity, folate metabolism, NADH/NADPH metabolism, thiol-mediated detoxification pathways, and redox-active metal ion metabolism. It is proposed that specific subgroups of human malignancies display distinct mitochondrial transformative and/or tumor signatures that may benefit from agents that target these pathways.

30168803.authors: Zhu Y, Dean AE, Horikoshi N, Heer C, Spitz DR, Gius D
30168803.title: Emerging evidence for targeting mitochondrial metabolic dysfunction in cancer therapy

abstract.text: While the understanding of the genomic aberrations that underpin chronic and acute myeloid leukaemia (CML and AML) has allowed the development of therapies for these diseases, limitations remain. These become apparent when looking at the frequency of treatment resistance leading to disease relapse in leukaemia patients. Key questions regarding the fundamental biology of the leukaemic cells, such as their metabolic dependencies, are still unresolved. Even though a majority of leukaemic cells are killed during initial treatment, persistent leukaemic stem cells (LSCs) and therapy-resistant cells are still not eradicated with current treatments, due to various mechanisms that may contribute to therapy resistance, including cellular metabolic adaptations. In fact, recent studies have shown that LSCs and treatment-resistant cells are dependent on mitochondrial metabolism, hence rendering them sensitive to inhibition of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). As a result, rewired energy metabolism in leukaemic cells is now considered an attractive therapeutic target and the significance of this process is increasingly being recognised in various haematological malignancies. Therefore, identifying and targeting aberrant metabolism in drug-resistant leukaemic cells is an imperative and a relevant strategy for the development of new therapeutic options in leukaemia. In this review, we present a detailed overview of the most recent studies that present experimental evidence on how leukaemic cells can metabolically rewire, more specifically the importance of OXPHOS in LSCs and treatment-resistant cells, and the current drugs available to target this process. We highlight that uncovering specific energy metabolism dependencies will guide the identification of new and more targeted therapeutic strategies for myeloid leukaemia.

34561557.authors: de Beauchamp L, Himonas E, Helgason GV
34561557.title: Mitochondrial metabolism as a potential therapeutic target in myeloid leukaemia

abstract.text: Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death that is regulated by the balance between prosurvival and proapoptotic BCL-2 protein family members. Evasion of apoptosis is a hallmark of cancer that arises when this balance is tipped in favour of survival. One form of anticancer therapeutic, termed 'BH3-mimetic drugs', has been developed to directly activate the apoptosis machinery in malignant cells. These drugs bind to and inhibit specific prosurvival BCL-2 family proteins, thereby mimicking their interaction with the BH3 domains of proapoptotic BCL-2 family proteins. The BCL-2-specific inhibitor venetoclax is approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and many regulatory authorities worldwide for the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and acute myeloid leukaemia. BH3-mimetic drugs targeting other BCL-2 prosurvival proteins have been tested in preclinical models of cancer, and drugs targeting MCL-1 or BCL-XL have advanced into phase I clinical trials for certain cancers. As with all therapeutics, efficacy and tolerability need to be carefully balanced to achieve a therapeutic window whereby there is significant anticancer activity with an acceptable safety profile. In this Review, we outline the current state of BH3-mimetic drugs targeting various prosurvival BCL-2 family proteins and discuss emerging data regarding primary and acquired resistance to these agents and approaches that may overcome this. We highlight issues that need to be addressed to further advance the clinical application of BH3-mimetic drugs, both alone and in combination with additional anticancer agents (for example, standard chemotherapeutic drugs or inhibitors of oncogenic kinases), for improved responses in patients with cancer.

34663943.authors: Diepstraten ST, Anderson MA, Czabotar PE, Lessene G, Strasser A, Kelly GL
34663943.title: The manipulation of apoptosis for cancer therapy using BH3-mimetic drugs

abstract.text: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death that is triggered by the toxic build-up of lipid peroxides on cellular membranes. In recent years, ferroptosis has garnered enormous interest in cancer research communities, partly because it is a unique cell death modality that is mechanistically and morphologically different from other forms of cell death, such as apoptosis, and therefore holds great potential for cancer therapy. In this Review, we summarize the current understanding of ferroptosis-inducing and ferroptosis defence mechanisms, dissect the roles and mechanisms of ferroptosis in tumour suppression and tumour immunity, conceptualize the diverse vulnerabilities of cancer cells to ferroptosis, and explore therapeutic strategies for targeting ferroptosis in cancer.

35338310.authors: Lei G, Zhuang L, Gan B
35338310.title: Targeting ferroptosis as a vulnerability in cancer

abstract.text: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are central players in the microenvironment of solid tumors, affecting cancer progression and metastasis. CAFs have diverse phenotypes, origins and functions and consist of distinct subpopulations. Recent progress in single-cell RNA-sequencing technologies has enabled detailed characterization of the complexity and heterogeneity of CAF subpopulations in multiple tumor types. In this Review, we discuss the current understanding of CAF subsets and functions as elucidated by single-cell technologies, their functional plasticity, and their emergent shared and organ-specific features that could potentially be harnessed to design better therapeutic strategies for cancer.

35883004.authors: Lavie D, Ben-Shmuel A, Erez N, Scherz-Shouval R
35883004.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts in the single-cell era

abstract.text: Maintenance of protein homeostasis and organelle integrity and function is critical for cellular homeostasis and cell viability. Autophagy is the principal mechanism that mediates the delivery of various cellular cargoes to lysosomes for degradation and recycling. A myriad of studies demonstrate important protective roles for autophagy against disease. However, in cancer, seemingly opposing roles of autophagy are observed in the prevention of early tumour development versus the maintenance and metabolic adaptation of established and metastasizing tumours. Recent studies have addressed not only the tumour cell intrinsic functions of autophagy, but also the roles of autophagy in the tumour microenvironment and associated immune cells. In addition, various autophagy-related pathways have been described, which are distinct from classical autophagy, that utilize parts of the autophagic machinery and can potentially contribute to malignant disease. Growing evidence on how autophagy and related processes affect cancer development and progression has helped guide efforts to design anticancer treatments based on inhibition or promotion of autophagy. In this Review, we discuss and dissect these different functions of autophagy and autophagy-related processes during tumour development, maintenance and progression. We outline recent findings regarding the role of these processes in both the tumour cells and the tumour microenvironment and describe advances in therapy aimed at autophagy processes in cancer.

36864290.authors: Debnath J, Gammoh N, Ryan KM
36864290.title: Autophagy and autophagy-related pathways in cancer

abstract.text: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) continues to have a poor prognosis, warranting new therapeutic strategies. The bone marrow (BM) microenvironment consists of niches that interact with not only normal haematopoietic stem cells (HSC) but also leukaemia cells like AML. There are many adhesion molecules in the BM microenvironment; therein, integrins have been of central interest. AML cells express integrins that bind to ligands in the microenvironment, enabling adhesion of leukaemia cells in the microenvironment, thereby initiating intracellular signalling pathways that are associated with cell migration, cell proliferation, survival, and drug resistance that has been described to mediate cell adhesion-mediated drug resistance (CAM-DR). Identifying and targeting integrins in AML to interrupt interactions with the microenvironment have been pursued as a strategy to overcome CAM-DR. Here, we focus on the BM microenvironment and review the role of integrins in CAM-DR of AML and discuss integrin-targeting strategies. LINKED ARTICLES: This article is part of a themed issue on Cancer Microenvironment and Pharmacological Interventions. To view the other articles in this section visit http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/bph.v181.2/issuetoc.

37258706.authors: Ogana HA, Hurwitz S, Wei N, et al.
37258706.title: Targeting integrins in drug-resistant acute myeloid leukaemia

abstract.text: Multiple myeloma (MM) the second most frequent hematological malignancy is typically preceded by asymptomatic precursor stages. Genetic alterations alone do not fully explain disease progression, as many are already present in pre-malignant stages, highlighting the critical role of the bone marrow microenvironment (BMME) in supporting malignant transformation, disease progression, and therapy resistance. BMME provide survival cues, mediate adhesion-dependent drug resistance, and orchestrate cytokine networks that protect MM cells from therapeutic stress. Despite the advances made in the past two decades, MM is, in most cases, still an incurable disease. The rising use of T cell redirecting therapy (CAR-T cells and bispecific antibodies) has increased awareness on the importance of the immune microenvironment. In this paper we will review the role of the different components of the BMME putting them in the context of novel therapy, with a special focus on T-cell redirecting therapies, with a glance at future perspectives and developments.

41178643.authors: Guadagno L, Schütt J, Brinkert K, Schenk T, Brioli A
41178643.title: The role of the bone marrow microenvironment in disease progression and drug resistance in multiple myeloma in the era of novel agents

abstract.text: It took decades from the discovery of BCL-2, initially identified in chromosomal translocations associated with lymphoid malignancies, to understand how BCL-2 and its family members regulate apoptosis, launching a transformative journey in cancer biology often called "the road to ruin". Developing powerful BCL-2 inhibitors for clinical use required decades. Yet, this remains as one of the most successful achievements in a field that started ~40 years ago, as recounted by its pioneers. BCL-2 was later found to inhibit apoptosis by preventing mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP), a breakthrough that clarified its role in cancer pathogenesis. Such effects of BCL-2 on MOMP prevent cytochrome c release and caspase activation, while its family members-anti-apoptotic proteins (e.g. BCL-2, BCL-XL) and pro-apoptotic proteins (e.g. BAX, BAK, BH3-only proteins)-orchestrate a delicate balance in cell death regulation. MicroRNAs like miR-15/16, often deleted in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), modulate BCL-2 expression, driving oncogenesis. Mechanistically, BAX/BAK oligomerization forms mitochondrial pores, with sublethal MOMP triggering inflammation via cGAS-STING and NF-κB pathways. Alternative MOMP inducers (e.g. BOK) and mitochondrial dynamics further refine apoptotic control. Clinically, the BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax has revolutionized CLL and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) treatment, showing efficacy in TP53-mutant CLL and elderly AML patients when combined with CD20 antibodies or hypomethylating agents. However, resistance, driven by BCL-2 mutations (e.g. Gly101Val) or MCL-1 upregulation, poses challenges. Limited success in solid tumors underscores the complexity of BCL-2 family dependencies. Future directions include novel inhibitors targeting MCL-1 or BCL-XL, BH3 profiling for precision therapy, and combinations with immune or DNA repair modulators. Non-apoptotic roles of BCL-2 in metabolism also warrant exploration. This review highlights the clinical success of BCL-2 inhibitors, addresses resistance mechanisms, and explores future directions, including sublethal MOMP, inflammatory outcomes, and novel inhibitors. Celebrating the collaborative, interdisciplinary efforts that transformed fundamental discoveries into life-saving therapies, this account underscores both the triumphs and the "potholes" encountered on the path to understanding apoptosis, while identifying open questions for ongoing research.

41714805.authors: Croce CM, Tait SWG, Garcia-Sáez AJ, et al.
41714805.title: What does BCL-2 do? From new molecular insights to the clinical implications

abstract.text: Myelodysplastic Neoplasms (MDS) are a group of clonal hematopoietic malignancies originating from hematopoietic stem cells. Their pathogenesis involves not only genetic abnormalities in hematopoietic cells but is also closely associated with functional dysregulation of the bone marrow microenvironment (BMME). In MDS, both the heterogeneous cellular populations and non-cellular components of the BMME exhibit significant dysfunction. Aberrant BMME components drive the initiation and progression of the disease through complex intercellular interactions. In-depth research into its pathological features and molecular mechanisms is of great significance for developing effective targeted therapeutic strategies. In recent years, novel treatment strategies based on BMME regulation have made significant progress, including immunomodulators, epigenetic regulators, molecularly targeted drugs, and cell therapies, providing new insights for improving the clinical outcomes of MDS patients. This article systematically reviews the pathological features of the BMME in MDS and its key molecular mechanisms in disease development, and discusses the latest clinical research advances in BMME-targeted therapies.

41816334.authors: Cong X, Peng X, Chen X, Wang N, Zhang L, Li L
41816334.title: Bone marrow microenvironment reprogramming in myelodysplastic neoplasms: from pathological mechanisms to targeted therapeutic strategies

abstract.text: Restoring apoptosis in malignant cells represents a central goal of anticancer therapy. Tumour cells often escape cell death by overexpressing anti-apoptotic members of the BCL-2 protein family, particularly BCL-2, BCL-xL, and MCL1. These proteins inhibit the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptotic pathway through intricate interactions with pro-apoptotic partners and direct modulation of the mitochondrial outer membrane. Their pivotal role in cell survival has established them as attractive therapeutic targets. Over the past two decades, significant efforts have been devoted to developing selective small-molecule inhibitors capable of neutralising these proteins and reactivating apoptosis. A first milestone was the discovery of ABT-263 (navitoclax), a dual BCL-2/BCL-xL inhibitor. Building on this achievement, the development of venetoclax, a highly selective BCL-2 inhibitor, marked a major breakthrough, demonstrating potent pro-apoptotic activity and clinical efficacy in several leukaemia subtypes. Despite these advances, the design of inhibitors of BCL-2 family members remains challenging, largely due to the structural characteristics of the BH3-binding groove, which is both shallow and hydrophobic, complicating the identification of molecules with optimal binding affinity and selectivity. PROTACs targeting BCL-xL may represent a promising future strategy, potentially overcoming the intrinsic limitations of small molecule inhibitors.

41937490.authors: Cilloni D, Ferrando A, Frassoni F
41937490.journal_full: Journal of cellular and molecular medicine
41937490.title: Targeting BCL-xL in Myeloid Malignancies: From Inhibitors to PROTAC

abstract.text: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has achieved transformative outcomes in B-cell malignancies but remains limited in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where antigenic heterogeneity, a suppressive myeloid-driven microenvironment, and a metabolically restrictive bone marrow niche collectively impair efficacy. In AML, CAR T-cell failure is driven not only by antigen escape but by a coordinated program of exhaustion encompassing transcriptional, epigenetic, metabolic, and functional dysfunction. The AML bone marrow niche further enforces dysfunction through suppressive immune populations, inhibitory cytokines, checkpoint signaling, metabolic competition, and impaired trafficking. This review outlines a "fitness-first" framework consolidating intrinsic and extrinsic determinants of CAR T-cell performance. Optimized manufacturing, cellular programming, and microenvironmental modulation provide a unified strategy to enhance CAR T-cell fitness and enable durable therapeutic responses in AML.

42440668.title: Modulating CAR-T cell exhaustion and fitness in acute myeloid leukemia: mechanistic metabolic and microenvironmental strategies

abstract.text: The BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax has transformed outcomes for older or frail patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and its resistance mechanisms are becoming better defined, including compensatory and lineage-associated switches toward MCL-1 or BCL-xL dependence, oncogenic signaling activation, blast phenotype, and differentiation stage. Additional putative mechanisms-such as emerging BAX mutations, mitochondrial structure remodeling, integrated stress response, and metabolic adaptations, including enhanced amino acid uptake and fatty acid oxidation to sustain oxidative phosphorylation-require further validation.

42575085.title: Beyond BCL-2: What drives venetoclax resistance in acute myeloid leukemia?

abstract.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) develops in a chronically injured liver where metabolic adaptation, oxidative stress, innate immune signalling, and immune tolerance are already intertwined. Mitochondria connect these processes: they sustain tumour-cell fitness, yet damaged organelles expose mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) as an intracellular and intercellular danger signal. Persistent reactive oxygen species, altered mitochondrial dynamics, nucleoid instability, and incomplete mitophagy-lysosomal clearance can oxidise, fragment, and displace mtDNA. The resulting material may remain in the cytosol, circulate freely or in protein-associated complexes, or be transferred within extracellular vesicles. These forms are not immunologically equivalent. Cytosolic mtDNA favours cGAS-STING access; endocytosed material can engage endolysosomal TLR9; and oxidised mtDNA can cooperate with mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, ATP, cardiolipin, and ionic perturbation in NLRP3 inflammasome-associated signalling. Redox remodelling also alters interferon responsiveness, inflammasome competence, and myeloid-cell metabolism, allowing recipient cells to assign different meanings to a similar mitochondrial signal. We integrate these mechanisms into an acute immune activation-chronic immune adaptation continuum. Transient, spatially restricted, and efficiently cleared danger can support antigen presentation and effector recruitment, whereas recurrent or poorly cleared signalling can become embedded in suppressive myeloid remodelling, lymphocyte dysfunction, and spatial immune escape. Direct HCC studies support treatment-induced mtDNA-STING activation, hypoxic extracellular-vesicle-mediated mtDNA transfer, macrophage TLR9 signalling, and TFAM-mtDNA-NLRP3 coupling. The transition between immune states remains a testable synthesis, not an established linear pathway. Therapeutic intervention should be matched to signal form, recipient-cell competence, timing, spatial context, and hepatic reserve; pathway activation alone is an inadequate guide.

42761405.authors: Chang Z, Liu G, Zhang J, Lei H, Quan H, Piao Y
42761405.title: Redox-driven mitochondrial DNA stress in hepatocellular carcinoma: innate immune remodelling, tumour immune escape, and immunotherapy implications

abstract.text: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) adapt to hypoxia, nutrient competition, lipid accumulation, and anticancer treatment. Mitochondria contribute to this adaptation through energy metabolism, redox signaling, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sensing, and metabolite-dependent regulation of gene expression. This Review examines mitochondrial dynamics, mitophagy, proteostasis, respiratory remodeling, and lipid-droplet interactions, distinguishing direct TAM evidence from findings in other experimental systems. Tumor studies link these processes to IL-12 and IL-10 production, interferon responses, antigen presentation, and lymphocyte recruitment, with effects that vary by pathway and macrophage state. These findings do not establish a single optimal level of mitochondrial quality control. We discuss how macrophage lineage, spatial niche, and treatment exposure may influence the response to mitochondrial interventions. Therapeutic development will require causal validation in defined TAM populations, selective delivery, and measurements of immune function alongside mitochondrial changes. Evidence in human TAMs and direct studies of organelle contacts remain limited. Somatic mtDNA variation is considered separately from altered gene expression and DNA release, with lineage-tracing evidence distinguished from functional causation.

42909308.authors: Xu J, Liu Y, Zhang H, et al.
42909308.title: Mitochondrial regulation of tumor-associated macrophage function

abstract.text: Macroautophagy (hereafter referred to as autophagy) is generally regarded as a cytoprotective process that maintains cellular homeostasis through intracellular recycling and metabolic adaptation. However, under certain conditions, autophagic machinery can contribute directly to cell death. Defining when autophagy functions as a cause rather than a consequence of cellular demise remains a major challenge and complicates the concept of autophagy-dependent cell death (ADCD). Experimental studies indicate that ADCD can occur through multiple mechanisms, including excessive self-digestion, autophagy-dependent lysosomal injury, selective autophagy-mediated degradation of critical cellular components, and specialized death programs such as autosis. These processes intersect extensively with apoptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis, placing ADCD within a broader network of regulated cell death pathways. Evidence from cancer, neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, and inflammatory diseases further suggests that ADCD contributes to pathogenesis and may provide therapeutic opportunities. In this review, we discuss the criteria for defining ADCD, the molecular mechanisms underlying its execution, its interactions with other cell death pathways, and its relevance to human disease. Together, we propose a practical framework for distinguishing bona fide ADCD from cell death merely accompanied by autophagy and provide guidance for establishing autophagy as a causal component of the death process.Abbreviations: AACD: autophagy-associated cell death; ADCD: autophagy-dependent cell death; ADF: autophagy-dependent ferroptosis; ATP: adenosine triphosphate; ATPase: adenosine triphosphatase; AUTACs: autophagy-targeting chimeras; BH3: BCL2 homology 3; CAR-T: chimeric antigen receptor T; cGMP: cyclic guanosine monophosphate; CMA: chaperone-mediated autophagy; DAMPs: damage-associated molecular patterns; DHA: dihydroartemisinin; ER: endoplasmic reticulum; ER-phagy: endoplasmic reticulum-selective autophagy; H2O2: hydrogen peroxide; HIV-1: human immunodeficiency virus type 1; I/R: ischemia-reperfusion; LMP: lysosomal membrane permeabilization; MTOR: mechanistic target of rapamycin kinase; PUFAs: polyunsaturated fatty acids; RHIM: receptor-interacting protein homotypic interaction motif; ROS: reactive oxygen species; sGC: soluble guanylate cyclase; SGLT2: sodium-glucose cotransporter 2; TCR-T: T-cell receptor-engineered T; UPR: unfolded protein response.

42921971.authors: Meng L, Dai M, Zhang X, et al.
42921971.title: A guide to autophagy-dependent cell death: concepts, criteria, and mechanisms

abstract.text: The network of transcription factors (TFs) is an integral component of executing macroautophagy/autophagy-lysosome gene expression to maintain cellular homeostasis. Across metazoans, conserved TFs, particularly the helix-loop-helix factor TFEB, convert upstream signals into specific genetic programs through mechanisms ranging from DNA recognition and chromatin remodeling to biomolecular condensates. The dysregulation of TF-governed gene programming disrupts the progression of metabolic disease and cancer, highlighting that dissection of transcriptional regulation makes it a promising therapeutic target. Consequently, instead of indirectly modulating the pathways in which they are involved, targeting these essential TFs directly is becoming a new trend for pharmaceutical development. In this review, we systematically elucidate current mechanisms of the TF-driven autophagic transcriptome, and summarize current small molecules targeting these TFs in various disease.Abbreviations: AD: Alzheimer disease; 42922083.authors: Qin W, Yang L, Deng X, et al.
42922083.title: Transcriptional control of autophagy: mechanisms, dynamics, and pharmacological modulation

abstract.text: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by phospholipid peroxidation and is increasingly recognized as an important vulnerability in cancer. Its sensitivity is determined by the interplay between membrane lipid composition, iron availability, oxidative stress, and antioxidant defense. Cancer cells can adapt to these pressures by altering the balance between polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fatty acids, thereby shifting toward either ferroptosis sensitivity or resistance. Emerging evidence indicates that alternative splicing provides an additional regulatory layer by generating functionally distinct isoforms of genes involved in cystine transport, iron metabolism, oxidative stress, antioxidant protection, and lipid remodeling. Functionally validated splice events affecting the cystine/glutamate antiporter subunit, transferrin receptor, spermidine/spermine acetyltransferase 1, SCL/TAL1 interrupting locus protein, and cluster of differentiation 44 demonstrate that isoform switching can influence ferroptotic susceptibility independently of total gene expression. This review integrates current knowledge on the biochemical basis of ferroptosis, the lipid determinants of ferroptosis sensitivity, and splicing-dependent mechanisms that shape vulnerability and resistance in cancer. Therapeutic strategies targeting ferroptosis defense systems, lipid metabolism, and alternative splicing are also discussed. Finally, we highlight the potential of integrating long-read ribonucleic acid sequencing, lipidomics, proteomics, and functional ferroptosis assays to develop multidimensional vulnerability signatures for patient stratification and precision cancer therapy.

42942016.authors: Procopciuc LM, Hangan AC, Lucaciu RL
42942016.title: Lipid Metabolism and Ferroptosis in Cancer: Regulatory Mechanisms, Alternative Splicing, and Therapeutic Implications

abstract.text: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) comprises a clinically and biologically heterogeneous group of breast cancers defined by the absence of estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor expression and the lack of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) overexpression or amplification. Although systemic treatment has expanded beyond chemotherapy to include immune checkpoint blockade, poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibition in selected patients with germline BRCA1/2 variants, and antibody-drug conjugates in advanced disease, therapeutic resistance and disease recurrence remain major challenges. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are abundant stromal cells that contribute to the organization and function of the TNBC microenvironment. Rather than representing a single uniformly tumor-promoting population, CAFs encompass transcriptionally and functionally diverse states that vary across tumors, spatial niches, and treatment contexts. Current evidence supports roles for selected CAF populations in extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, paracrine signaling, metabolic exchange, immune-cell positioning, and adaptation to therapeutic stress. Recent single-cell and spatial studies have further identified ECM-rich, inflammatory, hypoxia-associated, and progenitor-like fibroblast states that correlate with distinct immune landscapes and treatment responses. However, many proposed CAF markers are shared across states, nomenclature remains inconsistent among datasets, and most CAF-directed therapeutic strategies are supported primarily by preclinical evidence. This review summarizes the current understanding of CAF heterogeneity in TNBC, examines the mechanisms through which fibroblast states influence tumor progression and antitumor immunity, and critically evaluates their contribution to chemotherapy and immunotherapy resistance. Particular attention is given to the distinction between mechanistic evidence and associative transcriptomic findings, as well as to the translational challenges that must be addressed before CAF-based biomarkers or therapies can be incorporated into routine TNBC management.

42948317.authors: Wei S, Xie X, Cao Y, Wei L
42948317.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts in triple-negative breast cancer: heterogeneity, tumor-stroma crosstalk, and therapeutic resistance

abstract.text: Immune-checkpoint blockade has changed cancer therapy, yet durable responses remain limited by immune exclusion, myeloid suppression and metabolic adaptation within the tumor immune microenvironment. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of lipid-peroxidation-driven regulated cell death, offers a mechanistic bridge between tumor metabolism and antitumor immunity. Ferroptotic tumor cells can release danger signals, oxidized lipid mediators and antigenic material that shape dendritic-cell activation, macrophage behavior, myeloid-derived suppressor cell function and CD8+ T-cell responses. Based on currently heterogeneous evidence, we propose a working model in which acute and spatially restricted tumor-cell ferroptosis may favor immune priming and checkpoint sensitivity, whereas persistent or broadly distributed lipid-peroxidation stress may impair effector immune cells and sustain suppressive states. This temporal-spatial distinction remains incompletely validated in directly comparable experimental systems. This review summarizes the biochemical foundations of ferroptosis, the immune signals released by ferroptotic cells, the reprogramming of innate and adaptive immune compartments, and the emerging use of ferroptosis inducers, nanomedicines and immune-checkpoint combinations. We also discuss biomarkers, in vivo monitoring and immune-cell-specific toxicity as key barriers to clinical translation. A central conclusion is that ferroptosis should be treated not as a monolithic tumoricidal modality, but as a microenvironment-specific immune remodeling process whose therapeutic value depends on timing, localization and preservation of antitumor immune function.

42953155.authors: Shi Q, Tan B, Xing H
42953155.title: Ferroptosis in the tumor immune microenvironment: from danger signals to immune reprogramming

abstract.text: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are integral components of the tumor microenvironment (TME) and are increasingly recognized as critical regulators of nearly every hallmark of cancer. Once viewed as a uniform, protumorigenic cell type, it is now clear that CAFs comprise a spectrum of dynamic and plastic functional states with both tumor-promoting and tumor-restraining capacities. This functional duality, conceptualized within the framework of cancer as a "wound that fails to heal", is dictated by their diverse cellular origins, the specific activation pathways engaged (such as TGF-β and PDGF), and the evolving cues from the TME. In this Review, we dissect the multifaceted roles of CAFs, from their promotion of cancer cell proliferation, invasion and angiogenesis through secreted factors and extensive extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, to their profound influence on the immune landscape. We detail how distinct CAF subsets, such as myofibroblastic (myCAFs) and inflammatory (iCAFs) CAFs, orchestrate an immunosuppressive niche and contribute to therapeutic resistance. We also explore the compelling evidence for tumor-suppressive CAF functions, which have catalyzed a paradigm shift in therapeutic strategies-moving away from indiscriminate CAF ablation towards nuanced approaches aimed at reprogramming their state. These strategies include modulating key signaling pathways, normalizing the CAF-remodeled ECM, and exploiting unique metabolic vulnerabilities. Finally, we discuss how advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are resolving this complexity, paving the way for the development of precision therapies that can selectively neutralize pro-tumorigenic CAF activities while harnessing their beneficial functions to improve patient outcomes.

42957652.authors: Zhou L, Tang M, Wang K, et al.
42957652.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts: origins, functional heterogeneity and therapeutic potential
